newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine bonds not threatened by tax delay-market.
newsitem.headline: Argentine bonds not threatened by tax delay-market.

text.p: Argentine bond market players were unruffled Thursday by the failure of the lower house of Congress to pass the government plans to raise fuel taxes.

The failure by the Chamber of Deputies to muster a quorum to vote on the tax hikes was simply a reminder to markets of the slower pace of political reforms than during the first years of President Carlos Menem's rule, analysts said.
"This highlights what we already know, that there is not complete unity" on policy in the Peronist Party, said Esteban Thomsen, Argentina analyst at ING Barings.

Bonds initially slipped on the news but recovered during the day, helped by gains in other Latin American markets and U.S. Treasuries. The Senate approval by neighboring Brazil authorizing a buyback plan of Brady bonds to be swapped into other debt helped Argentine bonds firm as well.
"The signal to the markets is negative, but it is not final," said Hugo Diaz Lourenco, senior analyst at private consultancy C&E Consultores.

After waiting nearly a month for the implementation of the hike in fuel taxes to raise revenues to slash the budget deficit, traders said another week of delays would have little immediate impact on sentiment, which remains fairly buoyant.
The proposal is now expected to return to the Chamber of Deputies Wednesday.

"Failure to obtain (a) quorum for fiscal package vote should renew pressure on Argentine assets, but to the degree that shorts are set up on the delay, it likely presents a buying opportunity as we expect approval by early October," said IDEA financial consultancy in an investors note.

Bonds are likely to adopt a more flat trend but the "expectations that the measures will be approved will continue," said Lourenco. The delay still means the government will start collecting revenues to plug the deficit later. With the measures, this year's budget deficit is seen at $5 billion.

Ever since former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo was fired from his post in July, the market has become more aware of potential political delays. "This role of politics will be more common than before," said Thomsen.
"Any realistic examination of Congress shows this can happen."

Anyway, said traders, the separate Senate approval of the extension of the Fiscal Pact law, allowing the federal government to keep all the revenue from the fuel taxes without sharing it with the provinces, offset part of the let-down. "The Senate delivered and that is good news," said Thomsen.

One worry which could haunt the market though, is whether the signing of a letter of intent with the International Monetary Fund will now also be delayed. On Tuesday, Economy Minister Roque Fernandez said he expected the letter to be signed before the weekend.
